anchor: Disruption recovery in low-altitude logistics requires coordinating routes, departure times and charging across unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and shared facilities. This study examines how large language models coordinate these decisions to repair an existing delivery plan. We develop ARCO-Bench, an evaluation framework that combines optimized reference solutions with mission-event reconstruction under fixed vehicle assignments and mission sequences. Controlled diagnostic tasks isolate resource and preference effects, while independently generated networks link flight time and energy through an empirical power model. On the network tasks, admissible model-generated plans retain the optimal numbers of urgent and total missions, with most remaining quality gaps arising from changes to the incumbent plan. Minimum-change analysis identifies cross-UAV repairs beyond the evaluated local search neighborhood. The local optimizer attains reference quality on 23 of 36 network tasks; verified selection with generated plans increases this count to 31--33. Capacity and preference analyses further show how shared access and recovery priorities alter the preferred repair. These findings identify where generated plans complement local optimization and explain how scheduling and energy dependencies shape recovery quality.
replacement: Disruption recovery in UAV logistics couples route choice, departure timing and charging across mission chains and shared facilities. This study examines generated repairs through ARCO-Bench, combining optimized references with mission-event reconstruction under fixed vehicle assignments and sequences. The evaluation includes 72 controlled tasks, 36 network disruption tasks and 24 paired tasks with dispersed charging facilities. On the original networks, every admissible model plan retains optimal urgent and total service, while most quality gaps concern changes to the incumbent plan. Generated plans improve upon a fixed four-mission repair neighborhood, but a common 600-s comparison shows that iterative repair closes part of this gap and unrestricted optimization attains reference quality on all 60 network tasks. Recovery priorities explain much of the limited rerouting in the original plans: placing tardiness before plan-change cost induces waiting-to-rerouting transitions in seventeen tasks and increases on-time urgent completions from 245 to 263 of 294 demands. Longer closures induce the same transition in seven of twelve new network pairs, with four also changing charging. Restricted optimization and event traces identify when additional charging is necessary to preserve service after an energy-intensive detour. These findings locate the contribution of generated alternatives relative to local search and explain how operating priorities and route--energy dependencies shape repair quality.

\paragraph{Returned-plan failures.}
DeepSeek's three infeasible first-attempt plans violate either the charging
sequence or corridor reservations. Table~\ref{tab:s_new_failures} locates
each violation; all other first-attempt returned plans in this experiment
are admissible.

\begin{table}[htbp]
\centering\small
\caption{Event-level failures in the new first-attempt evaluation. Corridor counts refer to one-minute reservation windows. Energy values are measured immediately after each flight, before destination charging.}
\label{tab:s_new_failures}
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}lX@{}}
\toprule
Task & Violated operating condition\\
\midrule
Ladder M02-short & U04 reaches M014 and M015 with 18.516 and 16.275 Wh, below its 19.980-Wh reserve. The plan omits the preceding charge after M012.\\
Regions L01-long & M004/U02, M015/U05 and M023/U07 reserve V13$\rightarrow$V01 in $[4,5)$; three reservations exceed capacity two.\\
Regions L02-long & M012/U04, M016/U05 and M024/U07 reserve V01$\rightarrow$V13 in $[11,12)$; three reservations exceed capacity two.\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}
\end{table}

In Ladder M02, charging after M014 cannot repair the reserve violation on
arrival at M014. The two corridor cases satisfy continuous simultaneous
occupancy but exceed the specified reservation capacity.

Regions L02 under the longer closure illustrates the latter mechanism.
DeepSeek's first plan reroutes two missions and increases charging on U07,
but M012/U04, M016/U05 and M024/U07 all reserve corridor
$\mathrm{V01}\!\rightarrow\!\mathrm{V13}$ during $[11,12)$ min, exceeding
its capacity of two. Their actual corridor intervals are
$[10.677,11.253)$, $[10.498,11.074)$ and
$[11.677,12.253)$ min, respectively: at most two aircraft occupy the
corridor simultaneously, yet three uses touch the same booking window.
In the reference plan, M016 traverses the corridor one minute earlier,
removing its reservation from that window. The failure therefore concerns coordinating
shared corridor reservations after rerouting, despite feasible individual
battery trajectories and mission-chain timing.
